knowledge_point.title: Evaluating the Line Integral of a Function Over Curve Expressed as a Function of Y

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=e^{\frac{y}{2}}$ between $(\sqrt{2},\ln{\left(2 \right)})$ and $(\sqrt{3},\ln{\left(3 \right)})$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $\ln{\left(2 \right)}\le t\le \ln{\left(3 \right)}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle e^{\frac{t}{2}},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{e^{t} + 4}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=3 \left(e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{6} e^{- 2 t}=3 e^{t}\end{aligned}
$$
Here $(e^{t/2})^6e^{-4t/2}=e^{(6-4)t/2}=e^{2t/2}$ by the exponent laws.

Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}^{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}\left(3 e^{t}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{e^{t} + 4}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}^{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}\frac{3 \sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=e^{t} + 4$, so $\mathrm{d}u=e^{t}\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $6$ and $7$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{6}^{7}\frac{3 \sqrt{u}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[u^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{6}^{7} \\ &=\left(7 \sqrt{7}\right)-\left(6 \sqrt{6}\right) \\ &=- 6 \sqrt{6} + 7 \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating the Line Integral of a Function Over Curve Expressed as a Function of Y

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=6x$ between $(\frac{20}{3},2 \sqrt{10})$ and $(\frac{8}{3},4)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First solve the curve equation for $x$: $y^2=6x$, so $x=\frac{y^{2}}{6}$.

Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $4\le t\le 2 \sqrt{10}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle \frac{t^{2}}{6},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{t}{3},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{t}{3}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\frac{6 \left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)}{t}=t\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{4}^{2 \sqrt{10}}\left(t\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{4}^{2 \sqrt{10}}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=t^{2} + 9$, so $\mathrm{d}u=2 t\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $25$ and $49$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{25}^{49}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{6}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right]_{25}^{49} \\ &=\left(\frac{343}{9}\right)-\left(\frac{125}{9}\right) \\ &=\frac{218}{9}\end{aligned}
$$
